body: {"total":7,"records":[{"title":"A medicines prompt in structured nursing handoff and omitted medication information: a before-after study on two medical wards","authors":"Okonkwo-Hale R, Brandt-Oyelaran L, Szabo-Merritt A","year":2021,"venue":"Journal of Ward Handover Practice","doi":"10.5555/jwhp.2021.0142","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"Background: medication content is the part of nursing shift handoff most often omitted. Methods: we added a four-line medicines prompt (held doses, new high-alert medicines, same-day changes, pending pharmacy items) to the handoff sheet on two medical wards and compared 16 weeks before and after, reviewing 30 handoff sheets per ward per fortnight against the medication administration record. Results: handoffs with at least one omitted medication item fell from 41 percent to 22 percent. The change was similar for day-to-night and night-to-day handoffs. Median handoff duration rose by 40 seconds per patient. Conclusions: a short medicines prompt was followed by fewer omissions; a controlled evaluation is needed."},{"title":"Bedside versus station handoff and pharmacist-found medication discrepancies: an interrupted time series","authors":"Varga-Lindholm E, Adeyemi-Castro T","year":2019,"venue":"Tarnvale Nursing Review","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We moved nursing handoff from the station to the bedside on one medical ward and compared monthly counts of medication discrepancies found by the morning pharmacist over 14 months before and 10 months after the change, with a second ward as a comparison series. Discrepancy counts fell by about one third after the change, with no change in the pre-existing trend on the comparison ward. In observed bedside handoffs, patients corrected a nurse's statement about their medicines in 6 percent of cases. A new electronic medication record was introduced on the intervention ward during the same period."},{"title":"Structured handoff tools in inpatient nursing: a systematic review of effects on information omissions","authors":"Castellanos-Reid M, Pohl-Mensah D, Nakashima-Grey Y, Oduya-Berg F","year":2022,"venue":"Clinical Transitions Quarterly","doi":"10.5555/ctq.2022.0311","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We searched five bibliographic databases to 2021 for studies of structured nursing handoff tools that measured omitted information. Nineteen studies met the inclusion criteria; 15 reported fewer omissions with a structured tool, and medication content was the category most often improved. Only three studies had a concurrent control group and one measured adverse events. Effects were larger when the tool was combined with audit and feedback. Outcome definitions were too heterogeneous to pool, and most studies were at high risk of bias."},{"title":"Controlled evaluation of a handoff checklist on six medical wards: effects at three and seven months","authors":"Ferreira-Holt J, Mbeki-Larsen S, Quist-Adebayo P","year":2023,"venue":"Northfold Quality in Care","doi":"10.5555/nqc.2023.0077","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"Three medical wards introduced a bedside handoff checklist with fortnightly audit feedback and three comparable wards continued usual handoff; wards were allocated by manager preference. At three months, checklist wards had 18 percent fewer handoffs with a missed medication item than comparison wards. Audit feedback stopped after the fourth month, and by seven months the difference was no longer visible. Checklist completion fell from 85 percent to 52 percent over the same period."},{"title":"Night-time disturbance from bedside handoff: what patients on medical wards say about being woken","authors":"Linwood-Achebe C, Ruiz-Tanaka H","year":2020,"venue":"Medication Safety Letters","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We held structured conversations with 24 adult inpatients on two medical wards about bedside handoff. Patients valued hearing about their medicines and described the 19:00 handoff at the bedside as rarely a problem. The 07:00 handoff was sometimes felt to be intrusive, and several patients asked to be skipped when asleep. Conversations were held by ward staff, which may have discouraged criticism."},{"title":"Measuring missed medication reconciliation at nursing handoff: agreement between handoff sheet review and direct observation","authors":"Dembele-Short K, Osei-Warwick N, Halvorsen-Idowu B","year":2024,"venue":"Journal of Ward Handover Practice","doi":"10.5555/jwhp.2024.0019","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We compared two ways of detecting missed medication reconciliation items at nursing handoff on one medical ward: review of the written handoff sheet against the medication administration record, and direct observation of the handoff by a trained observer. Sheet review identified 81 percent of the missed items found by direct observation. Agreement between two sheet reviewers was good (kappa 0.78), and sheet review took about three minutes per handoff."},{"title":"Patient participation in bedside handoff among older adults with hearing or cognitive impairment: an observational study","authors":"Mwangi-Lorenz A, Petit-Oduya S","year":2022,"venue":"Tarnvale Nursing Review","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We observed 312 bedside handoffs on three medical wards and recorded whether the patient took part in the medicines discussion. Patients with hearing impairment took part in 31 percent of handoffs and patients with cognitive impairment in 18 percent, compared with 64 percent of other awake patients. An interpreter was used in 2 of 21 handoffs for patients with limited English. The authors recommend reporting outcomes separately for patients who cannot take part."}]}
